Charleston at a glance

Charleston grew up around its harbor, fed by three rivers (the Ashley, the Cooper and the Wando). It has more residents than any other South Carolina city and serves as county seat for Charleston County. Residents numbered 150,227 in 2020, against 120,083 a decade earlier, and the latest estimate is 159,423. Total area is 135.51 square miles, of which 115.03 is land.

One wrinkle: the city limits straddle two counties, Charleston and Berkeley. Whichever county holds your parcel supplies your assessor and treasurer, so read the name on your tax bill before dialing. The neighborhoods also vary a great deal: the downtown peninsula, West Ashley, Johns Island, James Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island each carry different flood exposure, parking rules and rental rules.

Flooding and your sale

Almost every Charleston sale involves a flood conversation. Elevation averages about 3 feet, and the city names the Stono, Ashley, Cooper and Wando, a string of creeks and the ocean as sources of flooding. A lot outside the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area can still suffer from local drainage trouble, unmapped floodplain or rising seas. The city's 2019 Flooding and Sea Level Rise Strategy advises planning for 2.0 to 3.0 feet of sea level rise over the next 50 years.

The city issues a Flood Hazard Information Letter that shows a property's flood zone. Send requests for elevation certificates and flood details to floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov. If you think the FEMA map is wrong, for example because the lot sits above the Base Flood Elevation or was filled, you can file a Letter of Map Change with FEMA. An elevation certificate sent along with a map request can be flagged for problems such as inadequate flood openings in a garage enclosure, so have it checked first. The city's Floodplain Mapping page explains the process.

Before listing, pull together the roof's age, repair invoices and a note of any past water damage. Storm history is a standard buyer question here.

Who bills the tax and when it is due

Valuation belongs to the Charleston County Assessor, and billing and collection belong to the Charleston County Treasurer. Real estate tax is due January 15 of the following year without penalty, and a U.S. postmark decides whether a mailed payment was on time (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

StepPenaltyRunning total
After January 153%3%
After February 1Additional 7%10%
After March 17Additional 5%, then to Delinquent Tax15%

Partial payments are refused, since state law does not permit them, and paying online adds a surcharge. Visit the Treasurer at 101 Meeting St., Suite 120, Charleston, SC 29401, phone (843) 958-4360. For how an unpaid balance is handled at closing, ask the Treasurer or your title company. After a refinance, forward the bill to the new lender so escrow covers it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the county reassessment works

The state works on a five-year reassessment cycle. Charleston County's newest notices went out August 20, 2025. The Assessor appraises about 190,000 real property parcels and 6,500 titled mobile homes.

When market value rises by more than 15%, the increase in taxable value is capped at 15% over the earlier figure. The cap limits value, not the bill, since millage can change. Newly added property, property with 2024 construction and property with a 2024 Assessable Transfer of Interest may be uncapped or only partly capped.

  • Any appeal has to be written, signed by hand and addressed to the Assessor.
  • The objection window is 90 days after notices are mailed.
  • If no notice was sent that year, the appeal period generally closes on the tax due date, typically January 15.
  • Later stages carry 30-day deadlines, and filing an appeal does not delay the bill.

Phone, email and fax do not protect your rights. The Assessor's office is at 4050 Bridge View Dr., Suite 100, North Charleston, SC 29405, phone (843) 958-4100.

The 4% rate and what happens when the owner moves

Homes lived in by their owners are taxed at 4% of fair market value, and all other real property at 6%. Nothing about the 4% rate is automatic. Under S.C. Code 12-43-220, the owner must own and occupy the home as a legal residence and be domiciled there. Properties without approval are billed at 6%, and a bill shows "QR4" when the 4% rate is in place. The application deadline is typically January 15.

The statute also bars renting the home for more than 72 days in a calendar year. An owner who loses eligibility has six months to tell the assessor, or faces a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus interest.

Sellers who moved out before listing should take note. If the house was rented out or left empty, the 6% rate can apply, and the figure needed at closing may surprise you.

Short-term rental rules

Charleston sorts short-term rentals into three categories, with a ceiling of one STR unit on any property. Category 1 is the Old and Historic District. Category 2 is the rest of the peninsula. Category 3 covers Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

  • All three require a further off-street parking space, on top of the two that zoning demands for each dwelling unit.
  • Category 1 needs a structure individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2 needs a building constructed at least 50 years ago.

The city points owners to its property eligibility quiz or shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov (city category page). If you are marketing a house with rental income, get the permit status confirmed in writing, since the rules depend on location.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with property tax owed

Owing tax does not block a Charleston sale. Closing usually pays the debt from your proceeds. Get the payoff from the Treasurer before signing a contract, as the figure jumps on February 1 and again on March 17.

Overpaid tax can be refunded on request for up to two years back, which helps a seller who was charged 6% while qualified for 4%. Keep copies of every notice and receipt so the Assessor can trace the years involved. A title company can often spot a rate mix-up in the payoff before it reaches your closing table.

  1. Ask the Treasurer's Office for the payoff.
  2. Confirm the legal residence status with the Assessor.
  3. Order the Flood Hazard Information Letter so the buyer can see the zone.
  4. Confirm with the Assessor that the address on the bill matches the address you will list under.
  5. Verify the short-term rental permit if rental income is part of your listing.

Frequently asked questions

When is Charleston County property tax due?

The last penalty-free day is January 15 of the following year. After it come 3%, then another 7% after February 1 and another 5% after March 17.

How long do I have to appeal my Charleston assessment?

Ninety days from the mailing of the notice, in a signed written objection sent to the Assessor. A phone call, email or fax will not protect your rights.

Is Charleston in more than one county?

Yes, the city reaches into both Charleston and Berkeley counties. The tax bill names the county that serves your parcel.

Can I sell my Charleston house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. Closing normally pays the back tax out of your proceeds. Request a payoff from the Treasurer first, since the 10% and 15% totals kick in after February 1 and March 17.

Does Charleston have a flood-zone disclosure tool?

Yes. The city provides a Flood Hazard Information Letter that lists the flood zone for a property. Contact floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov for elevation certificates.

Greenville city overview

The city of Greenville is the county seat, in the Upstate region of South Carolina beside Interstate 85. It had 70,720 residents in 2020 and an estimated 75,310 for 2025, against 58,409 in 2010. Population dipped for decades and then climbed quickly after 2010.

That recent run-up means many longtime owners have watched their blocks change, and investors call them often. Mill-era worker cottages, bungalows and brick commercial blocks make up a good share of the older housing. Their roofs, wiring and pipes often need attention, and plenty of owners would sooner sell as-is than repair and list.

Who bills property tax inside the city

There is no separate city tax office for this. Greenville County bills every address, and its Tax Collector sits in the South Building, Suite 1100-S (864.467.7050). Pay by January 15 and no penalty applies. For anything about how the city's own levy appears on your bill, ask that office.

DatePenalty step
January 163 percent added
February 27 percent more
March 175 percent more, plus $15.00 execution cost

The schedule is written into S.C. Code 12-45-180. The lien attaches to the property, so any balance left at sale gets settled from your proceeds when the deal closes.

Challenging a new value

Write to Real Property Services, Greenville County Square, Suite 1000 (864.467.7300). A notice that raises your value by $1,000 or more opens a 90-day objection period counted from the mailing date, per state law.

  • Include the tax map number, your reasons and the figure you think is fair.
  • Mail or hand-deliver it, because email and fax are refused.
  • No notice in hand? The default deadline is January 15.

After the county finishes its review, a 30-day clock starts for requesting a County Board of Assessment Appeals hearing. A loss there gives you 30 more days, counted from the written decision, to take the case to the Administrative Law Judge Division.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What changes when a Greenville house sells?

Selling normally triggers an assessable transfer. The property is valued again as of December 31 in the year of the deed change, the 15 percent increase cap no longer applies, and the buyer's new notice typically comes the following year.

Title on January 1 decides whose name is billed. A deed that changes later puts both names on that year's bill.

Owner-occupants can claim a 4 percent rate and a school-tax credit with an original-signature application filed by January 15. A landlord selling a rental to someone who will live in it therefore hands over a house that can qualify. A buyer planning the reverse, turning a home into a rental, will not get that treatment.

Recording takes place in Suite S-2100 at Greenville County Square, 301 University Ridge. The combined state and county charge under Title 12, Chapter 24 is $1.85 for each $500 of value.

Unpaid tax and the tax sale

Delinquency starts on March 17. An execution notice follows, and the house can be advertised for a public tax sale at the Greenville Convention Center.

A buyer at the sale does not own the house outright yet. For 12 months the former owner can redeem by paying what was owed plus costs and interest that rises over time. Once the year runs out, the bidder gets a tax deed that transfers only the county's interest, with no warranty.

Call 864.467.7050 for this year's sale schedule. A sale before the auction avoids all of this.

Steps to sell a Greenville house with a tax problem

Whether you are behind or inherited a house carrying an old bill, the order below keeps things moving.

  1. Get the exact amount owed from the Tax Collector. It shifts on January 16, February 2 and March 17.
  2. Locate the deed. With an inherited house, collect estate papers too, since title work tends to take longest.
  3. Check that a legal residence application was filed. A missed one can mean the house was billed at the higher rate.
  4. Hand the payoff to the closing agent, who pays the county out of your proceeds on closing day.

Someone paying cash and buying as-is will not demand repairs, so a cottage with tired plumbing or an old roof can still close. A vacant house that sat through a freeze should have its pipes checked before you list.

All of these offices belong to the county, so the same few calls cover any address in the city.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Paying the bill

The county accepts payment in person at the Tax Collector's office, by mail or online. Most payments post within three to five business days, which matters near January 15 or any other penalty date. Mail early, or pay in person, if the date is close.

Penalties come off only when the county made the mistake, and you need direct evidence of that. A late bill is not enough, so do not count on a waiver. If you believe the county erred, gather your documents before you call.

The execution cost is a flat $15.00 added at the March 17 step, on top of the 3, 7 and 5 percent penalties. Once that step arrives, the cheapest move is usually to settle the account quickly or sell before the sale is advertised.

Landlords and out-of-town owners

Owners of rentals close to downtown workplaces and campuses sometimes grow weary of tenant management. Selling does not demand a vacant or staged unit, but the lease must be addressed in the contract.

Tell buyers whether the house is close to a bus line, an interchange or downtown. I-85 skirts the southeast side, I-185 curves around the south, and I-385 connects downtown with I-26, so commutes vary widely by street.

Thinking of moving out but keeping the house? Ask Real Property Services what renting it does to your bill first. Both the 4 percent rate and the school-tax credit hinge on the home being your legal residence.

Dates and phone numbers to keep handy

  • January 1: whoever is owner of record gets billed.
  • January 15: payment deadline, owner-occupant application deadline, and the cutoff for an appeal when no notice was mailed.
  • January 16, February 2 and March 17: penalties step up.
  • March 17: delinquency and an execution notice.
  • 12 months after a tax sale: redemption ends.

Payments and payoffs: Tax Collector, 864.467.7050. Values, appeals and the owner-occupied rate: Real Property Services, 864.467.7300. Deeds: the Register of Deeds at Greenville County Square.

A payoff figure goes stale quickly because the amount grows on every penalty date. Request a fresh one once your closing date is firm.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Which office collects tax on a house within Greenville city limits?

The county Tax Collector. Call 864.467.7050; no penalty applies if you pay by January 15.

What if I sell in the middle of the tax year?

Any unpaid balance stays with the property, and the closing agent takes it from your proceeds. A deed that changes after January 1 puts both owners' names on that year's bill.

What is my window for disputing a Greenville value?

Ninety days from the mailing of a notice that raised value by $1,000 or more. If none was sent, plan on January 15, and put the objection in writing.

Does the city guide differ from the county guide?

Only in focus. The same county offices assess and collect for the city, and the county guide covers all of Greenville County.

Can I still sell a house that was auctioned for taxes?

Yes, while the 12-month redemption window is open. After it closes the bidder can receive a tax deed, so most owners sell ahead of the auction.

Florence city in brief

Florence serves as the county seat of Florence County. Its 2020 population was 39,899, tenth among South Carolina cities, spread over 23.49 square miles of coastal plain. Two hospital systems dominate the job market, McLeod Regional Medical Center (the Pee Dee region's biggest employer) and MUSC Florence (third biggest).

I-20 reaches its eastern end in Florence while I-95 passes through, and Florence Regional Airport is roughly 2 miles east of downtown. An owner living out of town can handle a sale without much trouble.

Who bills property tax inside the city limits

Inside the city, a single county bill covers everything. The county does the collecting for the City of Florence, and the city's levy is included. City Council fixes its millage by June 30 each year for the fiscal year that begins July 1.

The Florence County Auditor assesses vehicles, watercraft, aircraft and business personal property. Mail goes to the last known address, and the city points out that a missing bill does not cancel the tax. Report any new mailing address to the Tax Assessor's Office.

OfficeAddressPhone
County Treasurer180 N Irby Street843-665-3041
County Tax Assessor180 N Irby Street843-665-3056
County Auditor180 N Irby Street843-665-3088
Delinquent Tax Collection180 N Irby Street843-665-3095
City Finance Department3rd floor, City Center, 324 W Evans Street843-665-3162

County offices open weekdays, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The city explains its side on its property tax payments page.

Due dates and penalties

Real estate tax must be paid by January 15. Under Section 12-45-180, the state adds 3 percent on January 16, 7 percent more on February 2 and 5 percent more on March 17, which together make 15 percent plus collection costs.

Bills commonly arrive about October. A January 15 on a weekend or holiday generally shifts the deadline to the next business day. You can pay at the county complex, mail a check to 180 N Irby Street or use the county's PayStar portal. Cash should never go in the mail, and the county sends receipts back by mail.

Ownership changes get a narrow break. Penalties are waived by the treasurer when a house changes hands during the tax year, the notice reached only the old owner and the new owner got none in time. Few sellers qualify, so do not plan around it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Paying the bill without trouble

The simplest approach is to pay well before January 15, since a payment that arrives late carries penalties no matter the reason. If you pay by mail, wait for the receipt to come back, and keep it with your closing papers. If you pay online through PayStar, expect to receive a receipt by mail as well. Delinquent accounts are handled by a separate office, Delinquent Tax Collection, so a bill that has already turned past due needs a different phone call from a current one.

Sellers who closed during the year should also check whether the next bill is headed to the new owner. A bill sent to a former owner still carries the tax, and the question of who pays should be settled in the closing statement rather than left to a phone call afterward.

What a seller can do about an assessment

To dispute a value, write to the assessor within 90 days of the date the assessment notice was mailed. A notice is owed whenever a value goes up by $1,000 or more, and in reassessment years the deadline for sending them is October 1. No notice? You can appeal in writing whenever you like, though the appeal reaches the current year only if you file before the first penalty date.

Reappraisal comes every five years, with a parcel's rise limited to 15 percent across that span unless there is an assessable transfer of interest. Millage drops when values rise overall. Send written appeals to the Assessor's office, where a PDF form is also offered, and phone 843-665-3056 to learn which cycle and dates cover your parcel.

If taxes on a Florence house go unpaid

Real property and mobile homes with unpaid tax can end up at a county-run public sale, and fees pile up before that. Recent amounts include $20 for notices in March, $30 for certified mail of a levy in April, $25 for advertising in August and $60 for a land mortgage search in October.

The latest sale was set for October 5, 2026 in the parking garage at the County Complex. Redemption is open to an owner or a mortgage holder for one year and a day, with interest stepping up by quarter at 3, 6, 9 and 12 percent of the bid. Late solid waste fees add $25 if paid after March 16. A tax deed carries no warranty, and liens may remain.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to gather before you list

Pull together the latest tax notice, the receipt from your last payment and any assessment notice you received. Together they show your values, your tax and the mailing address on file. If the title came to you recently, keep the recorded paperwork handy as well.

Call the offices in a sensible order. The Tax Assessor handles address records and appeals, the Auditor handles bill calculation and penalties, the Treasurer takes payment, and Delinquent Tax Collection issues payoff amounts. Note each answer with the date so your closing agent can rely on it later.

Selling a Florence house that owes tax

A tax debt does not rule out a sale. Before you set a closing date, call 843-665-3095 for the payoff, and then have your title company show it on the settlement statement.

  1. Obtain the payoff. Penalties climb in January, February and March and costs grow through the year, so an old number may be wrong.
  2. Ask the Assessor where your bills are being mailed.
  3. With an escrowed loan, ask the mortgage holder what it has already paid.
  4. Call the City Finance Department, 843-665-3162, about how the city's share is shown on the bill.

A vacant house or one with deferred repairs can sell for cash without the repair list and showings of a retail listing. We buy as is, and all we need to begin is the address and your newest tax notice.

Preparing the house for inspection

Florence summers are long, hot and humid, which sends inspectors straight to the cooling system, the attic ventilation and the roof. They run the air conditioner and hunt for water stains, and damp crawlspaces draw attention too. Servicing the equipment and patching small leaks before listing costs less than a credit negotiated later.

Collect service receipts for the roof and air conditioner, and file them with the tax notice and the payoff letter. A tidy folder shows buyers and their lenders that the house was looked after and the tax picture is clear.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax for the City of Florence?

The county does it for the city. Florence County's Treasurer collects the City of Florence's real estate and personal property taxes on one combined bill.

When is the property tax deadline in Florence, SC?

The deadline is January 15, and the first 3 percent penalty lands on January 16. Further penalties arrive February 2 and March 17, reaching 15 percent plus costs.

Who sets the city's property tax rate?

The City Council, by June 30 each year, for the fiscal year starting July 1. The levy is paid through the county bill.

What if I never received a Florence tax bill?

The tax is still due. Mail goes to the last known address, so the Tax Assessor's Office should always have your current one.

Can I sell my Florence house if I owe taxes?

Yes, if the balance and fees are paid off at closing. Phone the Delinquent Tax Office at 843-665-3095 for a payoff before choosing a date.

Anderson city taxes and the county offices

Anderson, the city, serves as county seat. It sits in South Carolina's northwest corner, about halfway along I-85, and counted 28,106 residents in 2020 against 203,718 for the whole county. City and county are separate layers of government that share one cashier. County staff collect the city's tax bill, so it is the county Treasurer you phone.

Bills, due date and penalty steps

Expect the bill on October 1. Pay it by January 15 and no penalty applies. The place to pay is the Anderson County Annex, 401 East River Street, and the Treasurer answers at (864) 260-4033.

A bill paid after January 15 owes a 15 percent penalty, and that total is assembled from three state-law steps: 3 percent on January 16, 7 percent more on February 2 and 5 percent more on March 17. Beyond March 17 the treasurer may issue a tax execution for the taxes, penalties and costs.

You may pay at the Anderson or Powdersville counter, send a check, or go online, where cards bring a convenience fee. If your lender pays from escrow, pass the notice along to it.

Offices and dates

Anderson County offices and tax dates

Treasurer, Anderson office401 East River Street, Anderson 29624, (864) 260-4033, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
Treasurer, Powdersville office4 Civic Court, Powdersville 29642, closed for lunch, 12:00 to 1:00 p.m.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Assessment ratio and appeals

Your own home gets a 4 percent assessment ratio, and nearly everything else is at 6 percent. Nobody applies the lower ratio for you. File with the assessor after you move in, no later than January 15. Second homes, vacation homes and rentals do not qualify.

Disagree with your value? Four steps:

  • Within 90 days of the notice, deliver a written objection to the assessor with your own market value estimate and supporting papers.
  • After the assessor replies, 30 days remain to appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals.
  • After the board rules, another 30 days let you request a contested case hearing from the Administrative Law Court.
  • Still unresolved on December 31? Ask in writing for a bill set at 80 percent of the protested value.

Filing does not stop the clock on the due date or forgive a penalty. Use a separate form for each parcel, and sign it, because unsigned or unsupported forms come back.

How a sale changes the value

A sale almost always counts as an assessable transfer of interest. In the year after it, the buyer's value jumps to full fair market value and the 15 percent cap that shields long-time owners no longer applies. Deeds, trust conveyances and distributions under a will all count, with exceptions for certain family transfers and for foreclosures that happen before redemption runs out.

A buyer who will live in the house must file for the 4 percent rate. For a property that stays at 6 percent, there is a 25 percent ATI exemption form, which must be in by January 30 of the next year.

You, the seller, are largely unaffected. The bill for your year of sale uses the value already on the roll, and the buyer feels the reset next year.

Selling with taxes owed

Neglected taxes can lead to a delinquent tax sale. Following it, twelve months are open for redemption by the owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor, who must pay the taxes, penalties and costs plus interest on the bid amount, climbing by quarter from 3 percent to 12 percent.

Selling first is cleaner, because your closing agent settles the back taxes from the proceeds. Also, when title moved during the year and the new owner got no notice, the treasurer is directed by state law to waive penalties.

  • Get a payoff that stays good through closing day.
  • Find out from the attorney how this year's bill is split.

Cash sale when tax is due

Sell for cash and the tax comes out of the price at closing, leaving your wallet alone. Hand your attorney the newest bill and every past-due notice, and the attorney requests the payoff from the county Treasurer.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Anderson houses in whatever shape they are in: deferred repairs, tenants, inherited title. Describe the property, the amount owed and your timing, and we will say plainly if we can make an offer.

Before any buyer conversation, gather the newest bill, any past-due notice, the deed or estate papers, and a note of where tax mail has been going. Pass these to the attorney early, since the payoff letter takes time and must stay valid until closing.

What to bring when you visit

Visits to the Annex go faster with paper in hand: the tax notice or at least the parcel details, photo ID, and a check if you mean to pay on the spot. If you are acting for an estate or a relative, add the documents that show your authority to sign. Staff in Anderson work weekdays until 5:00 p.m., and the Powdersville office closes for lunch from 12:00 to 1:00 p.m., so plan the visit around that gap.

The Auditor at (864) 260-4027 sets the levy and takes homestead applications, and the Assessor at (864) 260-4028 handles values and the legal residence form. If your question is about a value or a rate, call those offices first, since the Treasurer only collects what the others have set.

A simple timeline for a sale

Work backward from closing. Early on, ask the Treasurer for a payoff and note its good-through date. If the sale will close between October 1 and January 15, the new year's bill is already out, so ask the closing attorney how it will be split. If closing lands after January 15, the penalty steps may already be adding to the balance, and a fresh payoff is needed.

At closing the attorney pays the tax from the proceeds and files the deed. In the weeks that follow, the buyer applies for the 4 percent rate on a home they will occupy, and the county resets the value in the year after the transfer. Keep your closing statement showing the tax payment in case any later notice arrives in your name. If you are unsure which year a notice covers, read the date on its face before you pay, because paying the wrong year leaves the real bill open and its penalties running.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When are Anderson, SC property taxes due?

By January 15. Bills are mailed October 1, and the 15 percent penalty is applied after January 15.

Where do I pay City of Anderson property tax?

At the Anderson County Annex, 401 East River Street, or at the Powdersville office, by mail or online. The phone is (864) 260-4033.

Do I get the 4 percent rate automatically after buying in Anderson?

No. The buyer files a legal residence application with the county assessor after moving in, and the deadline is January 15.

How long do I have to dispute an Anderson assessment?

Ninety days from the assessment notice, in writing. With no notice, an appeal received before January 15 counts toward that tax year.

Can I sell an Anderson house that has delinquent taxes?

Yes. The closing agent pays the back taxes, penalties and costs from your proceeds, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff that matches your closing date.

Columbia, SC Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in South Carolina

Columbia and the counties behind the bill

Columbia, the capital, counted 136,632 residents in 2020 and is estimated at 147,035 today. The city covers 140.68 square miles and sits mostly in Richland County, with pieces in Lexington and Kershaw counties. Government offices, the University of South Carolina and Fort Jackson anchor local jobs, and that mix supports plenty of rental housing.

Sellers should start with the county line. Whichever county mails your bill supplies the assessor, auditor and treasurer you will phone. Everything below describes Richland County's offices, so a house on the Lexington or Kershaw side needs a call to that county for its own dates and rules.

Richland County offices

Richland divides the work among three offices: the Assessor, who assigns value; the Auditor, who computes tax and prepares bills; and the Treasurer, who receives and distributes payments. All three work at 2020 Hampton St., Columbia.

OfficeLocationPhone
AssessorSuite 2058803-576-2640
AuditorSuite 2067803-576-2600
Treasurer2020 Hampton St.803-576-2250

Treasurer hours are weekdays, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Payment is available online, at the counter and by mail, and a monthly plan can be requested. Phone for your current bill and exact due date. Late charges follow state law, which tacks on 3% after January 16, then 7% more by February 2 and 5% more by March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

How to appeal a Richland County assessment

An appeal begins as a written objection to the Assessor, due 90 days after the date printed on the reassessment notice. In a year with no notice, the cutoff is the first penalty date on that year's real property bill. The statute sets the same 90-day period (S.C. Code 12-60-2510).

An online appeal portal is available. Disputes that the Assessor and taxpayer cannot settle go to the Board of Assessment Appeals. A representative must hold a power of attorney on Form SC2848, and entity-owned property requires articles of organization or an operating agreement.

Paper filings go to 2020 Hampton St., Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204. It is worth asking when the next notices will be mailed, since that date can shape when you list.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

If you disagree with the value: the paper trail

Good records make an appeal easier. Save the dated reassessment notice, since your 90 days count from that date. Describe the property in your objection, explain what is wrong with the value, and keep a copy that shows when you sent it. Filing through the online portal is fastest.

When an agent, attorney or relative files for you, attach the SC2848 form. When an LLC or similar entity holds title, attach its organizing papers. Incomplete paperwork can stall a filing while your deadline keeps ticking.

A hearing is about value or classification, so bring comparable sales or an appraisal if you have one.

Why Columbia rental owners pay more

South Carolina assesses a home lived in by its owner at 4% and everything else, including rentals and second homes, at 6%. Your bill shows which ratio you have.

The City of Columbia's 2022 competitive property tax plan went further. It put the effective tax rate on commercial and rental property at 2.92% of value in Richland School District One and 3.55% in District Two, and it found that rentals pay 3.9 times more than owner-occupied property. That was a city planning document, not a tax bill, so rely on your actual notice.

A house that stops being a primary residence moves to 6% as well, so an owner who moved out but kept the property may lose the lower rate before listing.

Unpaid taxes and the Richland County tax sale

Taxes left unpaid in Richland County can end at the annual tax sale, normally held in the fall. Recent sales took place at Township Auditorium, 1703 Taylor St., Columbia, with a backup day if the first day ran long.

To halt a sale, pay the whole amount at the Treasurer's office before 5 p.m. on the Friday that precedes it. At that point only cash or a certified bank cashier's check is taken, and personal, company and escrow checks are turned away. Opening bids equal the delinquent taxes and costs plus the current year's taxes, and buyers get the property as is, without warranty.

The redemption period under state law is 12 months from the sale (S.C. Code 12-51-90). Tax sale questions go to delinquenttax@richlandcountysc.gov, and payment plans can be requested at plannedpayment@richlandcountysc.gov.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a Columbia house with taxes owed

Tax owed on a house will not stop a sale. The balance can usually be paid from the proceeds, and the Treasurer can explain payoff timing before you pick a closing date.

  1. Identify the billing county: Richland, Lexington or Kershaw.
  2. Obtain the current bill and a payoff from the Treasurer.
  3. Check whether the house is billed at 4% or 6%.
  4. If the tax sale is close, remember the cash-or-cashier's-check rule.

A cash purchase can close quickly enough to get ahead of a tax sale and spares you repairs and showings. With a rental, an inherited house or an empty property, send us the address and your newest notice and we will say what we can offer.

A short checklist before you list a Columbia house

Settle three questions before the sign goes up. First, the county: a Columbia address may belong to Richland, Lexington or Kershaw, each with separate offices, dates and forms. Second, know the rate. Check your latest bill for either the 4% owner-occupied ratio or the 6% rate that applies to rentals, second homes and former primary residences. Third, know the balance. A Treasurer payoff tells your closing office what to wire, and it avoids a late scramble if the figure has penalties in it.

Buyers and lenders can see the same records, so a clear tax history helps a closing go smoothly.

If a payment plan is on the table, ask for it before the tax sale season rather than during it. The county accepts plan requests by email, and an approved plan gives you a schedule to show a buyer. If you plan to sell instead, ask the Treasurer whether a plan changes the payoff or only the timing, and get the answer in writing for your closing office, with the date it applies.

Finally, remember who may need to sign the paperwork. For an entity-owned or inherited house, the person who deals with the Assessor or Treasurer needs proof of authority, which usually means the same organizing papers or power of attorney the appeal process asks for.

Frequently asked questions

Which county do I pay property tax to if I live in Columbia?

Most of Columbia lies in Richland County, so the Richland County Treasurer bills you. Some parcels sit in Lexington or Kershaw counties, and your bill names the one that applies.

How long do I have to appeal my Richland County assessment?

Ninety days, counted from the date on the reassessment notice, to send the Assessor a written objection. If no notice went out, the deadline is that year's first penalty date.

Does Richland County offer a property tax payment plan?

Yes. A monthly plan can be requested through the county's property tax page, and plannedpayment@richlandcountysc.gov handles those requests.

Can I stop a Richland County tax sale?

Yes, if you pay everything owed before 5 p.m. on the Friday ahead of the sale. Only cash or a certified bank cashier's check is taken then.

Why is my Columbia rental taxed at 6%?

A rental, second home or vacant house misses the 4% legal residence rate, and the state assesses that property at 6%.

Rock Hill and York County

A Rock Hill house is assessed and billed by York County, so questions about a parcel go to the county and not to a neighboring town like Fort Mill, Tega Cay, Clover or Lake Wylie. In 2020 the city had 74,372 people, the most of any city in the county, and the 2025 estimate stands at 75,911.

Location helps demand. The city sits about 25 miles south of Charlotte on the Catawba River, with Interstate 77 serving it through exits 73 to 82 and Interstate 85 reaching it at exit 102.

Textile mills built the city, and employers like 3D Systems, Comporium Communications, Hyosung, Winthrop University and Rock Hill Schools carry it now. Housing runs from older mill streets to newer subdivisions, and the tax and code points below fit both.

How the county sets what you owe

Your bill begins with an appraised value times an assessment ratio, and use of the house sets the ratio. Four percent goes to a primary residence the owner lives in. Six percent goes to second homes, vacant land and commercial property.

Nobody gets the 4 percent ratio by default. The owner files with the county assessor before January 16, the first penalty date, certifying that the home is the legal residence and that no other home has the 4 percent rate.

  • A buyer who moves in within 90 days of closing can have the 4 percent ratio dated back to purchase.
  • Renting for more than 72 days in the tax year can disqualify the home, so landlords should check with the assessor first.
  • Selling is an assessable transfer of interest. The parcel gets reappraised, and the 15 percent cap on increases is lifted for the first year after the transfer.

Keep that in mind when pricing. The first bill a buyer sees can exceed yours.

Sellers can smooth this over by telling serious buyers early that the county will reappraise after the deed records. A buyer who plans to live in the house should expect to file the legal residence application soon after moving in, and one who plans to rent should budget for the higher ratio. Hearing this from you, before the contract, builds trust and avoids a complaint after the first bill arrives.

Due dates and late penalties

Payment is due between September 30 and January 15 under state law, and penalties begin the next day in three steps:

DatePenalty added
Starting January 163 percent
After the second day of FebruaryA further 7 percent
After March 17A further 5 percent, for a total of 15 percent of the original bill

From there the county treasurer may issue a tax execution, and the state's delinquent tax chapter governs further collection. Another provision requires waiving penalties in certain title transfers where the new owner never got timely notice. If you close near January, ask your closing attorney whether it applies.

Installments are an option too: five payments landing on the 15th of February, April, June, August and October, chosen by January 15.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to challenge an assessment

Your written objection is due 90 days after the assessor mails the assessment notice. From there every step runs on its own clock, and a missed one can end the appeal.

  1. Ask the assessor for a meeting during those 90 days. It should be scheduled within 30 days, or soon after.
  2. Within 30 days of the conference, file a written protest. A mailed answer usually follows in about 30 more days.
  3. Next stop is the York County Board of Assessment Appeals, which you reach by filing within 30 days of the response.
  4. Final stage: a contested case hearing at the state Administrative Law Court, requested within 30 days of the board's written decision.

In a year without a mailed notice, a written appeal can be made any time, and one filed ahead of the first penalty date counts for that tax year.

What happens to the tax when you sell

The bill stays attached to the land, so closing normally pays the seller's share out of proceeds. A transfer after assessment lets the auditor divide the bill between the old owner and the new one.

A South Carolina attorney has to oversee your closing. Because the State Bar counts drafting, closing and recording as the practice of law, the attorney or title company you hire will handle the proration and payoff.

Deed recording costs $1.85 for every $500 of price, of which $0.55 stays in the county. The contract names the payer.

Owners who are 65 or older, totally disabled or legally blind can apply for the state homestead exemption, worth the first $50,000 of value on county, school and city bills. Ask the assessor if your house already has it.

City code problems that follow a house to closing

Tall grass, junk and parked vehicles top the list, enforced by the city's Neighborhood Inspections office. Growth above 12 inches on an improved lot, or 18 inches on a vacant one, can draw a notice.

The city sends one courtesy notice a calendar year, giving 7 days for debris and grass and 15 days for vehicles. Tickets then follow every 7 days at $25, $50 and $100, to a maximum of $250. Cases that stay open can reach Environmental Court, held the third Wednesday of each month at 120 East Black Street, where fines can reach $1,087.50 or up to 30 days in jail.

If the city clears the lot, the owner gets the bill, and leaving it unpaid creates a lien. Title searches find liens, and they must be paid before closing. To ask about an open case, call Neighborhood Inspections at 803-329-7014 and give your name for your own address.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes or code problems open

Back tax won't stop you from selling. Closing takes the balance out of your proceeds, with the closing attorney handling the payoff, and any city code lien has to be cleared too.

A short checklist helps. Get the current bill from the county, ask Neighborhood Inspections if a case is open at the address, and confirm with the assessor whether the homestead exemption or the 4 percent ratio is on file. Give your closing attorney the answers early.

Condition is the other common snag. Roof, cooling and moisture findings in a buyer's inspection can reshape a deal, while a cash sale as is skips the negotiation over a repair list.

Timing and paperwork for a Rock Hill sale

Start with the date. A closing before January 15 pays only the base bill, while one between January 16 and the second day of February adds the first penalty. Later closings add the next steps, and after March 17 the account can head to execution.

Rock Hill owners who live on the older mill-era streets should pay particular attention to exterior upkeep, because grass, junk and vehicles are the items the city's inspectors write up. A weekend of cleanup before the listing photos costs far less than a lien.

Walk the property before listing. Look at the lawn, the driveway and any stored vehicles with the city's limits in mind, because a notice in the weeks before closing can turn into a lien the buyer's title search will find. Photos taken on a given day also help if you need to show the lot was in order.

Ask the closing attorney early which documents are needed: the deed, the payoff from the county and, if a lien exists, the city's release. Sellers who inherited the house should also confirm who may sign for the owner. A cash buyer can often work around a messy file because no lender is waiting on a clean appraisal.

Frequently asked questions

Which office sends the Rock Hill tax bill?

York County. Its assessor sets the value and its Tax Collection office bills and collects. Call for the current bill on your parcel.

What is the last day to pay Rock Hill property tax without a penalty?

January 15 is the cutoff. Penalties of 3 percent, 7 percent and 5 percent then stack on January 16, after the second day of February and after March 17.

How long do I have to appeal my Rock Hill assessment?

Ninety days from the assessor's mailing, in writing. Each later step has a 30-day deadline.

Can I sell a Rock Hill house if I still owe property tax?

Yes. Your proceeds cover the unpaid tax at closing, with the closing attorney arranging the payoff. A city code lien has to be cleared as well.

Does a new owner keep my 4 percent tax rate?

No. A sale triggers reappraisal and the buyer applies for the 4 percent rate. Moving in within 90 days lets the buyer have it dated back to purchase.

Myrtle Beach housing at a glance

Myrtle Beach sits in Horry County on the Grand Strand. The 2020 count was 35,682 people, and the 2025 estimate is 40,937. Older cottages stand near the oceanfront, while condos and subdivisions fill the inland side. Half the homes date from 1992 or earlier.

A town house might be a full-time residence, a retirement home or a vacation rental, and the tax code treats each one its own way. Owners who live on seasonal work or rental income also feel the January 15 bill, which arrives in a slow part of the year.

Coastal condition and what buyers check

Hurricanes are the biggest threat to a house on this coast. Buyers send inspectors to look at salt damage, wind-driven rain and flooding first, which means the roof covering, windows, siding, HVAC and crawl-space moisture.

Unrepaired storm damage can stop a mortgage cold, and that pushes some owners toward a cash sale. Dig out your insurance papers and flood zone status before listing. Buyers' lenders will want both.

Who bills Myrtle Beach property tax and where to pay

Real property tax for Myrtle Beach addresses is collected by the Horry County Treasurer. The owner of record gets a single bill covering the city, the county and the school district. Four Treasurer offices serve the area:

  • Conway (main): 1301 Second Avenue, Conway, SC 29526
  • Myrtle Beach: 332 Hinson Dr, Myrtle Beach, SC 29579
  • South Strand: 9630 Scipio Lane, Surfside, SC 29588
  • Stephen's Crossroads: 107 Hwy 57 North, Little River, SC 29566

Weekday hours run 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and (843) 915-5470 reaches the main line. Pay at the counter, mail a check, drop it in the night box, go online or call 843-428-2126. Cards cost extra in fees.

Questions about exemptions or a changed mailing address on real property belong with the Tax Assessor, (843) 915-5040. For homestead, ring the Auditor at (843) 915-5051.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

Pay the whole bill by January 15 of the year after the tax year. S.C. Code 12-45-180 adds penalties in three steps to anything postmarked later. A bill that never reached you does not excuse the late charge.

Payment datePenalty added
January 163 percent
February 27 percent more
March 175 percent more, then tax execution

The county runs an installment payment program. Every year the Treasurer also auctions delinquent properties at a public sale. Phone the office to learn when that sale falls and how installments are set up.

Second homes and rentals

A house other than your legal residence is assessed at 6 percent of fair market value, against 4 percent for a primary home. Leasing it out for more than 72 days a year also costs you the lower ratio.

The Myrtle Beach Area Chamber of Commerce maintains a calculator at mbtaxcalc.com, and the city has pointed homeowners to it. It shows a Tourism Development Fee credit that only owner-occupied homes inside city limits receive. For figures on your own parcel, ask the county.

The split shapes every sale. A vacation-rental investor and a full-time resident carry very different bills, and a buyer moving in has to apply for the 4 percent ratio ahead of the first penalty date.

Selling with taxes owed

Back taxes will not block a sale. The title company wires the Horry County balance out of your proceeds at closing, so long as the price is high enough. Get the payoff first, because the balance grows at each penalty step.

One sensible order:

  • Phone the Treasurer for the balance, plus a payoff figure good through closing.
  • Learn whether your parcel is already on the yearly tax sale list.
  • Give the payoff letter to the title company.
  • Check with the Auditor or Assessor how your legal residence status is recorded, because the next owner's bill depends on it.

Should a tax sale happen first, S.C. Code 12-51-90 lets the owner buy the property back within twelve months. Redemption interest steps up by quarter: 3 percent of the bid in months one to three, then 6, 9 and finally 12 percent in months ten to twelve.

A cash buyer needs no lender appraisal and no repair list, which helps when storm wear or a deadline is the problem.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

If the value looks wrong, put your objection in writing and send it to the assessor. The window under S.C. Code 12-60-2510 is 90 days, counted from the mailing of the assessment notice.

Assemble your evidence first: comparable sale prices, contractor estimates, damage photos and the notice itself. The Tax Assessor, (843) 915-5040, can say which form to use.

Legal residence and homestead

The 4 percent ratio belongs to a home that is someone's legal residence and is not rented out for more than 72 days a year. It does not apply automatically to a new owner. The application has to reach the county before the first penalty date, which is January 16 for a standard bill.

Sellers can help the buyer here. If you have lived in the house, make sure your own status is on file and ask the Assessor what the buyer will need to submit after closing. A missed filing means the 6 percent ratio for that year, and a bigger bill the new owner may blame on the sale.

Homestead is a separate question. The Auditor at (843) 915-5051 is the office to call about it.

What to bring when you call or visit

Packing a few things spares you a second trip to any of the four offices: photo ID, the property address, the latest tax bill if you have it, and the contract or closing date.

Each office has a lane. The Treasurer knows what is owed and when. The Assessor knows how the house is classified and how to object. The Auditor handles homestead. Note who you spoke with and when, then hand the figures to your title company.

Heirs and out-of-town owners can do much of this by phone. Because online payment exists, settling a balance rarely requires a drive to Conway.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Timeline for a quick sale

Count back from the next penalty date. Paying before January 15 keeps the bill at its base amount, while a closing that slips past January 16 triggers the first charge. Further steps follow on February 2, and on March 17 the Treasurer can move to tax execution.

Every sale moves through a contract, a title search, a payoff request and a closing. Taxes only cause trouble when a penalty date lands inside that stretch, so give the title company those dates up front and a revised payoff can follow if closing shifts.

If your parcel is headed to the annual sale, treat that day as a hard stop. After a sale, redemption takes twelve months and costs more each quarter. Closing beforehand is cheaper and simpler.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Myrtle Beach?

The county Treasurer. Local walk-ins can use 332 Hinson Drive in Myrtle Beach, and the main office is in Conway.

When is Myrtle Beach property tax due?

The deadline is January 15, and three penalty dates follow it.

Can I pay my Myrtle Beach property tax online?

Yes, with a check or a Visa, MasterCard or Discover card. Cards carry a convenience fee.

Do rentals in Myrtle Beach get the 4 percent rate?

Not once the home is rented more than 72 days in a year. It is then assessed at 6 percent.

Can I sell a Myrtle Beach house with back taxes owed?

Yes, as long as the sale price covers the debt. Request a payoff from the Treasurer and give it to the title company.
